exercises.title: SUM: add up a column
exercises.task: In J2, calculate the total sales of all eight employees.
exercises.hint: SUM takes a range. The sales figures are in D2 to D9.
exercises.explain: SUM adds every number in a range. =SUM(D2:D9) adds the eight sales figures. Ranges are written with a colon between the first and last cell.

exercises.title: AVERAGE: find the mean
exercises.task: In J2, calculate the average sales per employee.
exercises.hint: AVERAGE works just like SUM, on the same range.
exercises.explain: AVERAGE adds the numbers in a range and divides by how many there are. Empty cells and text are ignored.

exercises.title: MAX and MIN: highest and lowest
exercises.task: In J2, find the highest sales figure.
exercises.hint: MAX returns the largest number in a range.
exercises.explain: MAX returns the largest number in a range and MIN returns the smallest. Both ignore text and empty cells.

exercises.title: IF: hit or miss the target
exercises.task: In F2, show "Hit" if Ava's sales (D2) are at least her target (E2). Otherwise show "Miss".
exercises.hint: IF has three parts: the test, the value if true, the value if false. Text goes in double quotes.
exercises.explain: IF checks a condition. =IF(D2>=E2,"Hit","Miss") returns Hit because 52,000 is at least 50,000. In a real workbook you would copy this formula down to F9.

exercises.title: COUNTIF: count matching rows
exercises.task: In J2, count how many employees work in the Sales department.
exercises.hint: COUNTIF needs the range to check (the Dept column) and what to look for.
exercises.explain: COUNTIF counts the cells in a range that meet one condition. Text criteria go in quotes and are not case-sensitive.

exercises.title: COUNTIF with a number condition
exercises.task: In J2, count how many employees sold more than 50,000.
exercises.hint: Put the comparison and the number together in quotes, like ">50000".
exercises.explain: Number conditions in COUNTIF are written as text: ">50000", "<=30000" or "<>0". Three employees sold more than 50,000.

exercises.title: SUMIF: total by region
exercises.task: In J2, calculate the total sales for the East region.
exercises.hint: SUMIF(range to check, condition, range to add). Check the Region column and add the Sales column.
exercises.explain: SUMIF adds values that meet one condition. Note the order: the range to check comes first and the range to add comes last. SUMIFS, for several conditions, puts the sum range first.

exercises.title: AVERAGEIF: average for one group
exercises.task: In J2, calculate the average sales for the Sales department only.
exercises.hint: AVERAGEIF uses the same pattern as SUMIF.
exercises.explain: AVERAGEIF averages the values that meet a condition: here, the four people in the Sales department.

exercises.title: VLOOKUP: find a value by name
exercises.task: In J2, use VLOOKUP to find Chloe Park's sales.
exercises.hint: VLOOKUP(what to find, table, column number, FALSE). Sales is the 4th column of A2:E9.
exercises.explain: VLOOKUP searches the first column of the table and returns a value from the column you choose. Always use FALSE as the last argument for an exact match. Without it, VLOOKUP assumes the first column is sorted and can return the wrong row.

exercises.title: VLOOKUP from a second table
exercises.task: In J2, look up Ava's department (B2) in the bonus table G2:H4 and return her bonus rate.
exercises.hint: The lookup value can be a cell reference. The bonus rate is column 2 of G2:H4.
exercises.explain: Using a cell reference as the lookup value lets you copy the formula down the column. Ava is in Sales, so the result is 0.05, or 5%.

exercises.title: XLOOKUP: the modern lookup
exercises.task: In J2, use XLOOKUP to return Gia Russo's region.
exercises.hint: XLOOKUP(what to find, where to look, what to return).
exercises.explain: XLOOKUP takes a lookup column and a return column separately, defaults to an exact match, and can return values to the left of the lookup column. It is available in Excel 365, Excel 2021 and later, and in Google Sheets.

exercises.title: INDEX and MATCH together
exercises.task: In J2, use INDEX and MATCH to return Finn Hale's target.
exercises.hint: MATCH finds the row position of the name. INDEX returns the value at that position in the Target column. Use 0 in MATCH for an exact match.
exercises.explain: MATCH("Finn Hale",A2:A9,0) returns 6, his position in the list. INDEX(E2:E9,6) returns the 6th target. This pair works in every version of Excel and keeps working when columns are inserted.

exercises.title: IFERROR: handle missing values
exercises.task: In J2, look up the sales for "Zoe Kim" with VLOOKUP. She is not in the list, so show "Not found" instead of an error.
exercises.hint: Wrap the whole VLOOKUP inside IFERROR( ... , "Not found").
exercises.explain: VLOOKUP returns #N/A when it cannot find a value. IFERROR replaces any error with the value you choose. Use it carefully: it also hides genuine mistakes in a formula.

exercises.title: LEFT and FIND: extract a first name
exercises.task: In J2, extract Ava's first name from A2 using LEFT and FIND.
exercises.hint: FIND(" ",A2) gives the position of the space. You want every character before it.
exercises.explain: FIND returns the position of the space (4 in "Ava Chen"). LEFT(A2,4-1) returns the first 3 characters: Ava. This pattern works for any first name length.
